title: Astronomical Twilight Calculator: True Darkness
description: Find when true night begins and ends with the Astronomical Twilight Calculator — the Sun 18° below the horizon, for any place and date. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, in London on 22 October 2026 astronomical dawn begins about 05:43 and dusk ends about 19:46 (computed) — but around the June solstice London gets no astronomical night at all.
quick_answer: The Astronomical Twilight Calculator finds when the Sun passes 18 degrees below the horizon — the end of astronomical dusk and start of astronomical dawn, the boundaries of true night. Enter a place and date and read both times: the astronomer's definition of dark, computed not guessed.

At mid-northern latitudes, midsummer can erase astronomical night entirely — London has none around the solstice. Late autumn dates restore hours of it; this calculator shows which before you book.
Observatory first-light and last-light are astronomical events by definition. Schedules built on sunset alone overstate the dark by an hour or more each end.
Civil (6°), nautical (12°), astronomical (18°) — one staircase, three landings. Computing the deepest step makes the staircase's whole shape obvious.

At the June solstice the Sun's lowest point under London is only about 15° below the horizon — it never reaches 18°. Result: weeks where astronomical night simply does not occur, and the sky stays in nautical twilight all 'night'.

faq: Below about 18° the Sun's scattered light becomes negligible against natural sky brightness — the convention astronomers settled on and almanacs publish. It is a standard, not a cliff edge in the physics.
Why does my location get no result on some dates?
Because the event genuinely does not happen: the Sun never sinks 18° below your horizon that night (high latitude, near solstice). The calculator reports the absence rather than inventing a time.
How long does astronomical twilight last?
From the 12° crossing to the 18° crossing — commonly 30–40 minutes at mid-latitudes, far longer toward the poles where the Sun's path runs shallow.
No — this is solar geometry. A full moon can brighten an astronomical night considerably; pair these times with the Moon Illumination Calculator for the real observing forecast.
Yes: astronomical dawn is the morning 18° crossing coming up, astronomical dusk the evening crossing going down. Almanacs name them by the night they bound.
Does elevation change my dark time?

A high observer sees the Sun dip later and rise earlier — horizon dip deepens the geometry by roughly a degree per 3,000 m. The calculator uses the standard sea-level horizon; mountain observers gain a few minutes of twilight each end.
Times are computed for the place and shown in its local civil time, daylight saving included — the Sun ignores clocks, but your schedule should not have to.
